title: Building a rule-based memecoin bot (Solana) – what entry/exit patterns actually worked for you?
author: Lordpototoy
selftext:
Quick note first: this is about **Solana memecoins** (pump.fun / PumpSwap / Raydium), not stocks or forex.

I'm building a trading bot with the help of an AI agent, but the bot itself is **not an AI making decisions**. It's a fixed set of rules that runs the same way every time. Right now it's paper trading several variants side by side, with realistic fees, slippage and latency.

What I've learned so far: most simple setups lose once real costs are included, and copying profitable bot wallets doesn't work well because of latency.

For those of you who built something similar:

* What entry signals held up over time (volume, holders, buy pressure, age, something else)?
* Which exits worked best: time cuts, trailing stops, partial take-profits?
* How did you model costs and fills so the paper results matched live trading?

Tips from EVM chains (Base, BNB, ETH) are welcome too. Thanks!

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body: Before choosing between trailing stops and partial take-profits, I’d calibrate the fill model separately for [pump.fun/PumpSwap](http://pump.fun/PumpSwap) and Raydium. Record the quote seen at each paper signal, simulated submission latency, pool reserves, priority fee, and the executable output from the route at arrival time. Then run the same rules in live shadow mode without submitting orders and compare predicted versus observed slippage by token age and trade size. That should reveal whether an exit really holds up or only benefits from stale quotes, especially since copied-wallet entries are already failing on latency.

replies.author: Lordpototoy
replies.body: Really useful, thanks. In your experience, how big was the gap between predicted and observed slippage on fresh PumpSwap pools, and did it mostly scale with trade size or with token age? Did you find a size where it stops mattering (e.g. <0.25 SOL)?

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: I don't have live results of my own, so this is a testing approach. For paper-to-live matching, model priority fees, failed transactions and a latency distribution (not a single number), and take fills from the actual pool state at the time of the signal, since price impact on thin pools is the biggest hidden cost. For signals, hold out a later period and count every variant you tried, because on memecoins the survivors of a large search are mostly luck. The earliest filters that usually matter are pre-trade checks on the token (mint and freeze authority, liquidity depth, holder concentration, team wallets), and Cymetica's Safe Launch Check reads those on-chain for any token, which is a quick way to screen the rug-type failures out of your sample.

replies.author: Lordpototoy
replies.body: Thanks, the "count every variant" point hits home, I've tested a lot of combos. How would you adjust for that in practice: a stricter threshold, or something like a deflated Sharpe / haircut per variant tested?

comments.author: tradematesHQ
comments.body: Most simple setups die on costs, not signals, so calibrate the fill model per venue first. Log quote, latency, reserves and priority fee at each signal, then shadow-run live and compare predicted vs actual fills before trusting any exit rule.

replies.author: Lordpototoy
replies.body: Agreed. What's an acceptable predicted-vs-actual fill error before you'd trust paper results, like within 1%? 2%?

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: paper variants side by side with fees and latency already in is more care than most memecoin bots get. the catch on pump.fun is that your fill depends on how many other bots saw the same signal, and paper can't see them, so expect live to come in worse.

replies.author: Lordpototoy
replies.body: That's the part I worry about most. Is there any on-chain proxy for "how crowded" a signal is that I could log in paper, like the number of buys in the same slot right after the trigger? And roughly how much worse was live vs paper for you?

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: the count of buys landing in the same slot, or the next two after your trigger, is a decent proxy, and you can pull it from block data after the fact and log it beside each paper fill. I don't run anything on Solana, so I have no live vs paper gap of my own to give you, and I'd distrust anyone quoting one for pump.fun.
